In the Go design each interactive profile mounts the answerer of its carrier and binds the agents it creates; the headless command registers the cli answerer when a controlling terminal can be opened and --json is not set, and asks there, also for a subagent, because the runner answers for the root session (DH-ADR-CLI-7). In every other case no answerer is registered and an approval settles unavailable and is denied, which is the stated rule, not an omission. Proven by DH-T-CLI-12, DH-T-CLI-13 and scenario DH-E-CLI-2.
A Windows machine cannot be the remote host, and a lost operation is never replayed; provisioning and reconnect, the other two missing pieces, now exist.
justification: Partly removed, partly kept on purpose (audit finding Q3-2). Removed: the transport needs no control master or socket forwarding, so a Windows machine can be the local end (DH-ADR-SANDBOX-7); provisioning is one command, dsh ssh install (DH-ADR-SANDBOX-8); the connection fiber reconnects for new work under a budget (DH-ADR-SANDBOX-10). Kept, each stated by its record: DH-ADR-SANDBOX-8 says, as a scope boundary of that record, that the remote host is Linux or macOS and that dsh ssh install refuses a Windows remote with ssh/unsupported-remote (recommended default, not confirmed by the owner); DH-ADR-SANDBOX-10 keeps no replay, because replaying a change that may have happened is how data is lost.

reason: The remote helper does not run on a Windows remote host; the musl half of the upstream limit is gone.
justification: Removed: the helper is the statically linked dsh binary built with cgo off for every released target, so there is no glibc or musl split (DH-ADR-NATIVESYSTEM-3). Kept: DH-ADR-SANDBOX-8 states, as a scope boundary of that record, that the remote host is Linux or macOS (recommended default, not confirmed by the owner), because a Windows remote needs its own process-tree owner, token preparation, journal, pseudoconsole and command-line quoting on the remote machine, none of which is designed. The earlier resolved row called the Windows remote a P2 part; no deliverable carried it (audit finding Q3-2).

reason: A copy to the clipboard that has succeeded cannot be taken back.
justification: The earlier row called this not applicable because the Go design has no client plugin to dispose of, but the limit itself arises in any design, as the debt audit found (Q3-7): the browser's clipboard interface writes and reads, and has no operation that undoes a write another program may already have read (W3C Clipboard API and events). The Go UI copies a transcript with one user gesture in the page (DH-ADR-3); what was copied stays on the clipboard.

reason: The JavaScript guest runtime is dropped by DH-ADR-8, so there is no retained Node process whose variables a reset would clear: a script keeps no program state between calls.
The limit describes the evaluation modes of the Node vm guest runtime, which is dropped by DH-ADR-8; a script keeps state only in files it writes.
The marker asks how an image tool's result is adapted for a JavaScript program; the JavaScript guest runtime is dropped by DH-ADR-8, so no program result adaptation exists.
The marker concerns return types in the generated TypeScript SDK for programs; the guest runtime and its generated SDK are dropped by DH-ADR-8, and no TypeScript declaration is generated.

The limit describes how Node and its vm module load modules inside a guest program; the JavaScript guest runtime is dropped by DH-ADR-8 and its seam by DH-ADR-PTC-1, so the harness evaluates no JavaScript and a script's imports are the business of whatever interpreter runs it.

The limit is about the Node provider keeping a process and heap per owner between programs; that provider is dropped by DH-ADR-8 and DH-ADR-PTC-1, and a script's process ends with its hosting call or its workflow run.

The limit is about Node formatting guest objects before output is counted; the guest runtime is dropped by DH-ADR-8, so no guest values exist and a script's output is bytes read through a bounded ring.

The limit is about the guest keeping a JSON snapshot beside each tool result for inspect; the guest runtime is dropped by DH-ADR-8, so a nested call's result is printed once as JSON or text by the tool command.
The limit is about host metadata kept for every image object a retained JavaScript program acquires; the guest runtime is dropped by DH-ADR-8, so a script holds no image objects.

The limit describes the execution modes of the Node provider, which is dropped by DH-ADR-8 and DH-ADR-PTC-1. A script keeps state in files and the persistent shell tool is the stateful form; long work is a background job or a background workflow run.
The limit is a side effect of rewriting top-level await so that node:vm can run it; the guest runtime is dropped by DH-ADR-8, and the Go host neither parses nor rewrites script text.
The limit is V8 behaviour in a retained vm Script context; the guest runtime is dropped by DH-ADR-8, so no JavaScript context exists.
The limit lists the semantics of the scoped REPL evaluator; the guest runtime and its evaluators are dropped by DH-ADR-8 and DH-ADR-PTC-1.
The limit is about JavaScript values crossing vm realms; the guest runtime is dropped by DH-ADR-8, and a nested call's result crosses a process boundary as JSON text.

The limit is about live JavaScript objects kept in a provider's memory between programs; the runtime seam is dropped by DH-ADR-8 and DH-ADR-PTC-1, and the durable record is the session log and the files a script writes.

The limit says the JavaScript runtime seam ships no container provider; the seam is dropped by DH-ADR-8 and DH-ADR-PTC-1. Where a script runs is decided by the execution world, and a container would be a world provider of the execution and sandbox areas.

The limit is about a node:vm context whose withheld globals only guide script authors; the guest runtime is dropped by DH-ADR-8 and a workflow script is an ordinary program (DH-ADR-PTC-3), confined by the operating-system sandbox and the tool pipeline, which the model is told plainly.
The limit is about JavaScript error objects from another vm realm; the guest runtime is dropped by DH-ADR-8, and a script sees a failed call as an exit status and one JSON error object with a code.
The marker asks for redeclaration warnings in the scoped REPL evaluator; the guest runtime and its evaluators are dropped by DH-ADR-8 and DH-ADR-PTC-1.

The team/message/queued records exist upstream so that logs written by earlier upstream releases stay readable. Reading upstream sessions in the store is dropped by DH-ADR-11 (a separate, one-way import of the current format only) and DH-ADR-2; the Go design has no team mailbox type, so there is no historical message to leave undelivered.

The limit describes Linux payloads that upstream's build downloads and locks for the workspace-dependencies tool. The tool is dropped by DH-ADR-CONTEXT-3, and the Go project builds and carries no payload (DH-ADR-15).

The limit describes executable permissions of a payload carried by upstream's Python wheel or desktop installer. The tool is dropped by DH-ADR-CONTEXT-3, and no payload is built or carried in the Go design.

It describes the node-tar library failing to load in the experimental browser-worker preview of the JavaScript host. That preview runtime is dropped by DH-ADR-17, and the Go host reads archives with the standard library.

The message_feedback sidecar is an earlier upstream storage format. Reading upstream formats is dropped by DH-ADR-2 and DH-ADR-11 (only upstream's current session format, through a separate import command), and the Go design never had a sidecar, so there is nothing to migrate.

The limitation describes the desktop start-up component and its shared owner peer for the desktop lifetime. The desktop application is dropped by DH-ADR-18, so the component and its limit cannot arise.
